, in patients with carpal-tunnel syndrome, a reduction in forearm segment motor conduction velocity of 5 m/s or more, below a value of 50 m/s, is likely to be associated with a neuropathy of some degree of severity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the majority of patients with carplal tunnel syndrome, the slowing in forearm segment of the motor conduction is due to the carpal tunnel compression.

in patients with uncomplicated compression of the median nerve at the carpal canal, the reduction in forearm motor conduction velocities may not be a reliable index of the severity of the compression, and the reduction in mixed nerve conction velocities is not a useful indicator of the presence or absence of a widespread neuropathy.

the forearm segment of median nerve is not a good indicator of the severity of compression in the carpal tunnel, and that a reduction in motor conduction in this segment may be a feature of more widespread sensorimotoneuropathy in some cases of carpal tunnel syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in patients with carpal syndrome, a slow motor conduction velocity in the median nerve forearm segment does not necessarily indicate the presence of a generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
, in the presence of a sensorimotor neuropathic process, slow motor condcution velocity in the forearm can be explained by slowing of the mixed nerve.
the conduction velocity in the arm segment of the median can be reduced in the absence of any evidence of a more generalized sensorimotor neuropathic process.
